description:
Hello, Space Apps! 
We're a team Galactic Poet 

MT Asfi, our team lead, keeps us all pointed at one star. Developer Md. Ramjan Miah turns wild ideas into working code. Cartoonist Atasi Sharma gives anything a face and a reason to care. Editor Susmita Ghosh knows where every cut should land. Operations lead Zihad Rahman makes plans real.

Measure like engineers. Tell it like poets. That's why they call us Galactic Poet.
summary: Planes, trains, even space shuttles retire to museums. But when a rover retires on the Moon or Mars, it just stays there, and its name ends up as a quiet line on a data sheet. Not anymore! We built Rover-Villa, a digital museum and youth community that turns NASA's records into real life stories of these explorers. Read them as storybooks, watch them as cartoons, play them as games, or pull the machines apart in 3D, learning the science each one made possible. Find us at rovervilla.space, on Instagram (@rover_villa), and at Jagannath University, Bangladesh, where our community meets today. We grow with every mission, because even a machine far from home deserves to be remembered.
details:
For as long as we've been human, we've kept the things that mattered.

We gave museums to the first airplanes, to the steam trains that crossed continents, to the space shuttles that touched orbit and came home. You can stand beside them, look up, and say thank you.

But some of our bravest explorers will never get a museum.

Since the 1960s, we've sent machines where no human could follow. They touched the Moon before we did. They rolled across Mars for years, through dust storms and freezing nights, sending home postcards from worlds we had only dreamed of. And when the work was done, there was no ride home. They're still out there, right where they stopped.

Back here, each one slowly fades into a quiet line on a data sheet. A name. A date. "Mission ended." And to a kid, a line says nothing.

We think they deserve more than a line. So we built Rover-Villa.

A museum that fits in a pocket

A museum stays in one place. These machines are scattered across two worlds. So we built one that travels.

Rover-Villa is a digital museum and memorial for the rovers, landers and probes we left on the Moon and Mars. Every machine gets a home, and a life story told chapter by chapter, from the cleanroom where it was born to the last signal it sent.


From a NASA record to a story

NASA kept careful notes on every mission: catalog entries, mission pages, photographs, 3D files, planetary data. Written for scientists, they hide stories nobody has told yet. We read them like engineers and retell them like poets.

Then we ask each machine three questions. What were you built to do? What happened to you out there? What do we know now because you went? The answers become a chapter, a comic, a cartoon, a game.

A broken wheel, a big discovery

In 2006, one of Spirit's front wheels stopped turning. Spirit didn't. It kept going, dragging the dead wheel through the Martian dirt, and the wheel scraped the top layer away. Underneath was something bright: soil of almost pure silica, a sign that hot springs or steam vents once worked there, and with them, water.

On a data sheet, that's a broken part. In Rover-Villa, it's the day a broken wheel led Spirit to one of its greatest finds. Hardware, trouble, discovery: one story a kid can retell at lunch.

One machine, four doors

Every kid learns differently, and what you care about, you remember. So every machine has more than one door, and each one is free to open.

  • Read its life as a comic or a storybook, and let the browser read it aloud.
  • Watch Rover Villa Jr, our cartoon about the town where rovers go when the work is done.
  • Play the real science: keep Spirit and Opportunity alive through dust storms, read marsquakes like InSight, fly Ingenuity through air so thin nobody knew if anything could fly there.
  • Explore 3D models, many from NASA's own files. Spin them, pull them apart, print your own.


Real facts, imagined voices

Kids deserve stories that are fun and true, so we draw a clear line. Every fact comes from a NASA record, with its source right on the page. The machines speak, but their voices are imagined, and we say so. A teacher can teach from it. A parent can check every line.

Not just a website. A community.

A museum is more than its walls. It's the people who walk through, and what they talk about on the way out.

RoverVilla lives online and offline at once. On https://rovervilla.space, for anyone, anytime. On Instagram (@rover_villa), where our reels and comics drop in between one scroll and the next. And at Jagannath University in Bangladesh, where our community meets face to face: a machine's story on the big screen, its 3D model, its games, and a room full of questions. People learn together, then carry the stories home, reaching people who would never open a data sheet. That's how a community grows.

What we hope to achieve

The story isn't finished, and neither are we. Artemis is taking NASA back to the Moon, and every new mission will leave new machines, and new stories, behind. Rover-Villa will be there to tell them.

Next: these stories in Bangla and more languages, so kids can read them in the language they dream in. More schools and campuses beyond Jagannath University. And free classroom kits, so any teacher can host a Rover-Villa session.

Because even a machine far from home deserves to be remembered.


How we built it

  • Website: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Node.js, Tailwind CSS, Cloudflare
  • 3D and games: Three.js, GSAP
  • Stories and art: made by our team in Adobe Illustrator, After Effects, Premiere Pro, Blender and Canva, with AI image tools as one helper
  • Data: NASA mission and archive records, linked on every page
